meta.name: Power BI
meta.examFormat: Practical TPs · Power Query · DAX · Reports
meta.description: Microsoft Power BI — data import, Power Query, DAX, visualizations

chapters.title: Orientation — What is Power BI and why does it exist?

lessons.title: 1. What is Power BI?
lessons.html:
• Power BI is a business intelligence (BI) tool made by Microsoft. It lets you connect to data, clean it, model it, and turn it into interactive reports and dashboards.
  • It is used by analysts, students, and companies to answer questions about their data visually — instead of staring at rows of numbers in a spreadsheet.
  • Example: a sales manager wants to know which product sells best each month, in which region, compared to last year. Power BI turns a raw Excel file into an interactive chart they can click and filter in seconds.
  • Three parts of Power BI:
    • Power BI Desktop — the Windows app where you build everything. This is what you install and use for TPs.
    • Power BI Service — a website (app.powerbi.com) where you publish and share reports.
    • Power BI Mobile — a phone app to view published reports.
  • Important: Power BI Desktop only runs on Windows. For TPs you need a Windows machine. This course teaches you the concepts and logic so you can work in the real software confidently.

lessons.title: 2. Power BI vs Excel — what's the difference?
lessons.html:
• Both tools work with data, but they are designed for different things.
  • Excel = a spreadsheet. You manually type, edit, and calculate in cells. Good for small datasets, formulas in cells, one-off calculations.
  • Power BI = a reporting engine. You connect to data (you don't edit it directly), clean it automatically, and build visual dashboards that update when the data changes.
  • Key differences:
    • Excel struggles with millions of rows. Power BI handles them easily.
    • In Excel you change the data itself. In Power BI you write transformation steps that are re-applied every time the data refreshes.
    • Power BI reports are interactive — slicers, filters, drill-down. Excel charts are mostly static.
    • Power BI has a dedicated formula language (DAX) for calculations across tables. Excel uses cell formulas.
  • When to use which: Use Excel for quick personal analysis. Use Power BI when you need recurring reports, big data, or interactive dashboards for a team.

lessons.title: 3. The Power BI workflow — 4 stages
lessons.html:
• Every Power BI project follows the same four stages. Understanding this before touching the software saves a lot of confusion.
  • Stage 1 — Connect: Tell Power BI where your data lives (a CSV file, an Excel file, a website, a database). Power BI reads it without modifying the original.
  • Stage 2 — Transform (Power Query): Clean and reshape the data before loading it. Remove junk rows, fix data types, rename columns, pivot/unpivot. This happens in the Power Query Editor.
  • Stage 3 — Model: Define relationships between tables (like linking a sales table to a products table by product ID). This is the Data Model.
  • Stage 4 — Visualize: Build charts, tables, and dashboards on the Report canvas. Add slicers so users can filter interactively.
  • Trap: Many beginners skip Stage 2 and jump straight to building charts on messy data. The chart will be wrong. Always clean first.

lessons.title: 4. The Power BI Desktop interface
lessons.html:
• When you open Power BI Desktop you see three main views, switched by icons on the left sidebar:
  • Report view (default) — the canvas where you drag visuals and build your dashboard. Most of your time is here.
  • Data view — shows your loaded tables as a spreadsheet. You can browse data and write calculated columns here.
  • Model view — shows all your tables as boxes with lines connecting them. You manage relationships here.
  • The ribbon at the top has tabs: Home, Insert, Modeling, View, Optimize, Help. Each tab shows relevant buttons.
  • The Filters pane (right side) — add filters that apply to visuals, pages, or the whole report.
  • The Visualizations pane (right side) — choose chart types and configure which fields go on which axis.
  • The Fields pane (right side) — lists all your tables and columns. Drag them onto the canvas or into visuals.
  • Key button: Transform Data in the Home ribbon — this opens the Power Query Editor where all data cleaning happens.

lessons.title: 5. What is Power Query?
lessons.html:
• Power Query is the data-preparation engine inside Power BI. It is where you clean, reshape, and transform your data before it enters the model.
  • Think of it as a recorded set of instructions. Every transformation you apply gets recorded as a step. When Power BI refreshes the data, it replays all those steps automatically.
  • Power Query has its own editor — the Power Query Editor — which opens as a separate window inside Power BI Desktop.
  • Key parts of the Power Query Editor:
    • Queries pane (left) — lists all your data sources (queries). Each imported file or table is one query.
    • Data preview (centre) — shows the current state of the data after all applied steps.
    • Applied Steps pane (right) — the list of every transformation you've done, in order. You can click any step to see what the data looked like at that point.
    • Formula bar (top) — shows the M expression for the selected step.
    • Ribbon — tabs for Home, Transform, Add Column, View.
  • Trap: Changes made in Power Query Editor are not saved to your report until you click Close & Apply. If you close without applying, your changes are lost.

lessons.title: 6. M language — a first look
lessons.html:
• Everything you do in Power Query Editor generates code in a language called M (officially: Power Query Formula Language).
  • You don't need to write M yourself at first — the UI generates it for you. But reading it helps you understand what's happening and fix errors.
  • Every M query has the same structure:
    let
    Source = Csv.Document(...),
    Step2 = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source),
    Step3 = Table.RemoveColumns(Step2, {"OldCol"})
in
    Step3
  • let starts the query. Each line defines a step — a name, then =, then what it does.
  • in tells Power Query which step is the final output.
  • Each step uses the previous step's result as its input. This is why step order matters — delete a step in the middle and later steps break.
  • You will see M code in the formula bar when you click a step in Applied Steps. You don't need to memorize syntax now — just understand the shape.

lessons.title: 7. DAX — a first look
lessons.html:
• DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is Power BI's calculation language. You use it to write measures and calculated columns in the data model.
  • DAX is completely separate from M. M transforms data before it loads. DAX calculates on data after it loads.
  • Simple example:
    Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
    This measure adds up every value in the Amount column of the Sales table.
  • M vs DAX — when to use which:
    • Use M (Power Query) for cleaning, reshaping, importing — anything that changes the shape or content of the table.
    • Use DAX for calculations, aggregations, comparisons — anything that computes a value from existing columns.
  • Common beginner mistake: Creating a calculated column in DAX when a transformation in Power Query would be cleaner and faster. If you're changing data structure — use Power Query. If you're calculating a new value from existing columns — use DAX.

chapters.title: Data Fundamentals — tables, types, nulls, and messy data

lessons.title: 1. What is data?
lessons.html:
• Data = recorded facts or observations. A temperature reading, a sale amount, a student's grade, a product name — all data.
  • In Power BI, data almost always lives in tables. A table is a grid: rows going down, columns going across.
  • Row (also called a record) = one complete observation. One sale, one student, one product.
  • Column (also called a field or attribute) = one property shared by all rows. All the names, all the prices, all the dates.
  • Cell = the intersection of one row and one column. Contains one value.
  • Header = the first row of a table that names each column. Power BI needs headers to know what each column means.
  • Example — a sales table:
    OrderID | Product  | Amount | Date
1       | Laptop   | 1200   | 2024-01-15
2       | Mouse    | 25     | 2024-01-16
3       | Keyboard | 45     | 2024-01-16
    3 rows, 4 columns, 12 cells.

lessons.title: 2. Structured vs unstructured data
lessons.html:
• Structured data = data that fits neatly into rows and columns. CSV files, Excel tables, database tables. Power BI works best with structured data.
  • Unstructured data = data with no fixed format. Emails, PDFs, images, free-text comments. Power BI cannot directly analyze this.
  • Semi-structured data = has some structure but not a perfect table. JSON, XML, HTML pages. Power BI can import these but may need extra transformation.
  • Your professor's datasets are all structured — CSVs with clear rows and columns. This is the most common format in university TPs.
  • Rule of thumb: If you can open it in Excel and it looks like a table, Power BI can import it directly. If it looks like a document or a web page, it needs more work.

lessons.title: 3. Data types — what kind of value is in each column?
lessons.html:
• Every column in Power BI has a data type. The type tells Power BI how to store, display, and calculate with that column's values.
  • Text (called Whole Number, Decimal, Text, Date, etc. in the UI) — the most common types:
  • Text — letters, words, names, codes. Cannot do math on it. "Laptop", "Ahmed".
  • Whole Number — integers, no decimal point. 10, 42, -5.
  • Decimal Number — numbers with decimal points. 3.14, 19.99.
  • Date — a calendar date. 2024-01-15. Enables time-intelligence calculations in DAX.
  • Date/Time — date + time. 2024-01-15 09:30:00.
  • True/False — a boolean. Only two possible values.
  • Trap: Power BI auto-detects types on import and often gets it wrong. A column of sales amounts stored as Text cannot be summed. Always check and correct data types in Power Query before loading.

lessons.title: 4. Null values — what does empty mean?
lessons.html:
• Null = the absence of a value. Not zero, not an empty string — literally nothing. A cell that was never filled in.
  • Power BI shows nulls as null in the data preview (lowercase, grey).
  • Why nulls are a problem:
    • A SUM of a column containing nulls ignores the nulls — sometimes that's right, sometimes it's wrong.
    • A filter for a specific value will not match nulls.
    • Joining two tables on a column with nulls produces unexpected results.
  • What to do with nulls:
    • Remove rows that have nulls in critical columns.
    • Replace nulls with a default value (e.g. 0 for sales amounts, "Unknown" for names).
    • Keep them if the absence of data is itself meaningful.
  • Trap: null ≠ 0. A product with 0 sales sold nothing. A product with null sales has no data recorded — that's different.

lessons.title: 5. Duplicates and dirty data
lessons.html:
• Duplicate rows = the same record appearing more than once. If a sale is recorded twice, your total will be wrong.
  • Dirty data = data with errors, inconsistencies, or junk. The most common types:
  • Inconsistent casing: laptop, Laptop, LAPTOP — Power BI treats these as three different products.
  • Extra spaces: "Laptop" vs " Laptop" — the leading space makes them different. Use Trim in Power Query to fix.
  • Wrong data type: dates stored as text, numbers stored as text.
  • Merged fields: "Ahmed Ben Ali" in one column instead of separate First Name / Last Name columns.
  • Inconsistent formats: dates as 15/01/2024 in some rows and 2024-01-15 in others.
  • Rule: Spend 70% of your Power BI project time cleaning data. A clean model with simple visuals is worth more than a beautiful dashboard built on dirty data.

lessons.title: 6. CSV files — your most common data source
lessons.html:
• CSV = Comma-Separated Values. A plain text file where each line is a row and commas separate the columns.
  • Your professor's files are all CSVs. Example from unpivot.csv:
    Product,January,February,March,April
Laptop,10,15,12,18
Mouse,30,25,40,35
  • The first line is usually the header. Each subsequent line is one row.
  • Delimiter = the character that separates values. Usually a comma, but can be a semicolon (;) in French/European files, or a tab.
  • Trap: French Windows saves CSVs with semicolons as the delimiter (because commas are used as decimal separators in French). If your CSV looks like one giant column in Power BI, change the delimiter in the import dialog.
  • Encoding: If you see strange characters like Ã© instead of é, the file is UTF-8 but Power BI loaded it as a different encoding. Change encoding to UTF-8 in the import settings.

chapters.title: Importing Data — connecting Power BI to your files

lessons.title: 1. Get Data — the starting point
lessons.html:
• Get Data is in the Home ribbon. Click it and a dialog lists every source type: CSV, Excel, Web, SQL Server, and more.
  • Most common for TPs: Text/CSV, Excel Workbook, Web (URL), SQL Server.
  • After selecting a source, Power BI previews the data and offers two buttons: Load or Transform Data.
  • Rule: Almost always choose Transform Data — it opens Power Query Editor so you clean before loading. Load skips cleaning entirely.

lessons.title: 2. Importing a CSV file
lessons.html:
• Steps: Home → Get Data → Text/CSV → browse to file → Open.
  • In the preview dialog check: File Origin (UTF-8 for French files), Delimiter (Comma by default; change to Semicolon for French CSVs), then click Transform Data.
  • Your three professor CSVs (pivot.csv, unpivot.csv, transpose.csv) all use comma delimiter and UTF-8 — defaults work.
  • Trap: French Windows saves CSVs with semicolons as separator. If all data appears in one column, change the delimiter.

lessons.title: 3. Importing an Excel file
lessons.html:
• Home → Get Data → Excel Workbook → select file. A Navigator dialog shows all sheets and named tables.
  • Prefer named Tables over sheets — they don't include junk rows above the data.
  • Click Transform Data to open Power Query.
  • Trap: Excel files with merged cells, logos, or title rows above data import junk. Remove top rows in Power Query: Home → Remove Rows → Remove Top Rows.

lessons.title: 4. Importing from a web page
lessons.html:
• Home → Get Data → Web → paste URL → OK. Power BI fetches the page and shows all tables found.
  • Your professor provided this URL for practice:
    https://publicholiday.co.nz/nz-public-holidays-2021.html
    It has a table of NZ public holidays — import it and practice changing the Date column type, removing columns, and sorting.
  • Trap: Web sources break if the page changes structure. This is normal — web import is less stable than file import.

lessons.title: 5. Load vs Transform Data — the critical choice
lessons.html:
• Load → imports immediately with Power BI's guessed types. Fast but risky.
  • Transform Data → opens Power Query Editor. You clean before loading. Always safer.
  • When done in Power Query: Close & Apply saves all steps and loads data. Close (without Apply) discards all changes.
  • Habit: Always choose Transform Data on import. Check types. Remove junk. Click Close & Apply. Then build visuals.

chapters.title: Power Query Editor — the data-cleaning workspace

lessons.title: 1. The Power Query Editor layout
lessons.html:
• Power Query Editor has 5 zones:
  • Queries pane (left) — lists every query. Each CSV/Excel/web table is one query.
  • Data preview (centre) — current state of data after all applied steps.
  • Formula bar — M expression for the selected step.
  • Query Settings pane (right) — query name (Properties) + Applied Steps list.
  • Ribbon (top) — four tabs: Home, Transform, Add Column, View.

lessons.title: 2. Applied Steps — your transformation history
lessons.html:
• Applied Steps records every transformation as a named step. Auto-created steps on import: Source, Promoted Headers, Changed Type.
  • Click a step → preview data at that point. Delete (✕) → remove the transformation. Rename → double-click the name.
  • Trap: Deleting a step that a later step depends on breaks those later steps with a formula error.

lessons.title: 3. The formula bar and reading M
lessons.html:
• Click any step → formula bar shows the M expression:
    = Table.RemoveColumns(#"Previous Step", {"OldColumn"})
  • You don't write M from scratch yet — the UI generates it. But reading it helps you understand and debug.
  • Advanced Editor (Home → Advanced Editor) shows the full M script for editing directly.
  • Habit: After every transformation, click the step and read the formula bar. This is how you learn M naturally.

lessons.title: 4. Essential column operations
lessons.html:
• Rename: double-click column header.
  • Remove: right-click header → Remove. Or keep what you want: right-click → Remove Other Columns.
  • Change type: click the type icon left of column name → select new type. Always do this — never rely on auto-detect.
  • Split column: Transform → Split Column → By Delimiter.
  • Merge columns: Ctrl+click two columns → Add Column → Merge Columns.
  • Tip: Use Remove Other Columns (keep what you want) when there are many junk columns — fewer clicks.

lessons.title: 5. Essential row operations
lessons.html:
• Filter rows: dropdown arrow on column header → check/uncheck values.
  • Remove top N rows: Home → Remove Rows → Remove Top Rows → enter N.
  • Remove blank rows: Home → Remove Rows → Remove Blank Rows (removes rows where ALL cells are null).
  • Remove duplicates: select column(s) → right-click → Remove Duplicates.
  • Trap: Remove Blank Rows only removes rows where EVERY cell is null. Use Filter Rows on a specific column to remove rows with null in that column.

lessons.title: 6. Replacing values, Trim, and Fill
lessons.html:
• Replace Values: Transform → Replace Values. Leave 'Value to Find' empty to replace nulls.
  • Trim: Transform → Format → Trim. Removes leading/trailing spaces.
  • Capitalize Each Word: Transform → Format → Capitalize Each Word. Fixes 'laptop'/'LAPTOP'/'Laptop'.
  • Fill Down: Transform → Fill → Down. Fills null cells with the value above them.
  • Order matters: Trim before comparing. Capitalize before deduplicating. Change type before filtering by number range.

chapters.title: Transformations — Pivot, Unpivot, Transpose with real data

lessons.title: 1. Wide vs long format — the fundamental concept
lessons.html:
• Wide format: each category gets its own column. Easy to read, hard for Power BI.
    Product  | January | February | March
Laptop   |      10 |       15 |    12
  • Long format: one column for the category name, one for the value. Power BI works best with this.
    Product  | Month    | Sales
Laptop   | January  |    10
Laptop   | February |    15
  • Rule: If months, years, or categories are column headers → they're values → Unpivot to make them rows.

lessons.title: 2. Unpivot — wide to long (unpivot.csv)
lessons.html:
• unpivot.csv has months as columns. Problem: you can't filter by month in a chart.
    Product  | January | February | March | April
Laptop   |      10 |       15 |    12 |    18
  • Steps:
    1. Ctrl+click January, February, March, April headers.
    2. Right-click → Unpivot Columns.
    3. Rename Attribute → Month, Value → Sales.
  • Result: 20 rows (5 products × 4 months).
    Product  | Month    | Sales
Laptop   | January  |    10
Laptop   | February |    15
  • Trap: Select ONLY the month columns. If you include Product, it also becomes rows — wrong.

lessons.title: 3. Pivot — long to wide (pivot.csv)
lessons.html:
• pivot.csv is in long format. Goal: make each month a column for a comparison report.
    Product  | Month    | Sales
Laptop   | January  |    10
Mouse    | January  |    30
  • Steps:
    1. Click the Month column header.
    2. Transform → Pivot Column.
    3. Values Column = Sales. Aggregate = Sum.
    4. Click OK.
  • Result: 4 rows (one per product), one column per month.
    Product  | January | February | March
Laptop   |      10 |       15 |    12
  • Trap: Pivot on the column whose values become headers (Month), not the values column (Sales).

lessons.title: 4. Transpose — rows become columns (transpose.csv)
lessons.html:
• transpose.csv: subjects are columns, students are rows. After transpose, subjects become rows.
    BEFORE:
Student | Math | Physics | CS
Ahmed   |   15 |      14 | 18

AFTER (then promote headers):
Subject  | Ahmed | Sara | Youssef | Mariam
Math     |    15 |   17 |      12 |     18
Physics  |    14 |   16 |      13 |     17
  • Steps:
    1. Transform → Transpose.
    2. Home → Use First Row as Headers.
    3. Rename Column1 → Subject.
  • Always use First Row as Headers after Transpose — the original headers move to row 1.

lessons.title: 5. When to use which transformation
lessons.html:
• Unpivot: column headers are values (months, years, categories) → need them as rows for filtering/charting.
  • Pivot: a category column's values should become column headers → comparison table.
  • Transpose: the whole table is rotated the wrong way — rows should be columns and vice versa.
  • Quick test:
    • Are column headers actually values? → Unpivot
    • Spread a column's values into headers? → Pivot
    • Whole table oriented wrong? → Transpose
  • Real TP tip: Your professor's filenames tell you the operation: unpivot.csv → Unpivot, pivot.csv → Pivot, transpose.csv → Transpose.

chapters.title: M Language — reading and writing Power Query code

lessons.title: 1. What M is and why it exists
lessons.html:
• M (Power Query Formula Language) is the language that runs behind every transformation you apply in Power Query Editor. Every click generates M code automatically.
  • You don't write M from scratch at first — the UI generates it. But reading M helps you understand what's happening and fix errors.
  • Why M exists: Power BI needs a way to record transformations as a reproducible script so they can be re-applied every time the data refreshes. M is that script.
  • Where you see M: Formula bar (one step at a time), Advanced Editor (full script), error messages.
  • Goal for now: Read M confidently. Modify small parts. Write basic custom steps. Full M authoring comes with experience.

lessons.title: 2. The let / in structure
lessons.html:
• Every M query has the same skeleton:
    let
    Source = Csv.Document(File.Contents("file.csv"), ...),
    PromotedHeaders = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source),
    ChangedTypes = Table.TransformColumnTypes(PromotedHeaders,
        {{"Product", type text}, {"Sales", type number}})
in
    ChangedTypes
  • let starts the block. Each line is: StepName = expression.
  • Each step uses the previous step's result as input — that's why order matters.
  • in StepName declares the final output — what gets loaded into the model.
  • Step names can contain spaces if wrapped in #"Step Name":
    #"Removed Columns" = Table.RemoveColumns(Source, {"Junk"})
  • Trap: If you rename a step, every later step that references the old name breaks immediately.

lessons.title: 3. Common M table functions
lessons.html:
• These are the M functions Power BI generates most often. Reading them becomes natural quickly.
  • Table.RemoveColumns(table, {"col1", "col2"}) — removes named columns.
  • Table.RenameColumns(table, {{"Old", "New"}}) — renames columns.
  • Table.TransformColumnTypes(table, {{"col", type number}}) — changes data types.
  • Table.SelectRows(table, each [Sales] > 0) — filters rows. each means 'for each row'.
  • Table.PromoteHeaders(table) — uses first row as column names.
  • Table.Transpose(table) — transposes the table.
  • Table.UnpivotOtherColumns(table, {"Product"}, "Month", "Sales") — unpivots all columns except Product.
  • Table.Pivot(table, List.Distinct(table[Month]), "Month", "Sales") — pivots Month column.
  • Tip: When you apply any of these via the ribbon, click the resulting step and read the formula bar. This is how you learn M naturally.

lessons.title: 4. The 'each' keyword and row context
lessons.html:
• each is M shorthand for a function that runs once per row. It gives you access to the current row's values via _ or column names in square brackets.
  • Filter rows where Sales > 10:
    Table.SelectRows(Source, each [Sales] > 10)
  • Add a custom column that doubles Sales:
    Table.AddColumn(Source, "DoubleSales", each [Sales] * 2)
  • Conditional column:
    Table.AddColumn(Source, "Category",
    each if [Sales] > 20 then "High" else "Low")
  • Trap: Column names in M are case-sensitive. [sales] and [Sales] are different columns. If you get a 'column not found' error, check the exact casing.

lessons.title: 5. Reading and editing M in the Advanced Editor
lessons.html:
• The Advanced Editor (Home → Advanced Editor) shows your full M script in one editable window. Use it to:
  • Rename a step — change the name in the let block AND update all references to it in later steps.
  • Add a step manually — add a new line in the let block referencing the previous step.
  • Copy a query — copy the full M script and paste it into another query.
  • Example — manually adding a sort step:
    let
    Source = ...,
    Clean = Table.RemoveColumns(Source, {"Junk"}),
    Sorted = Table.Sort(Clean, {{"Sales", Order.Descending}})
in
    Sorted
  • Trap: M is whitespace-sensitive in some contexts. Keep each step on its own line. End every step with a comma except the last one before in.

chapters.title: Data Modeling — tables, keys, and relationships

lessons.title: 1. What is a data model?
lessons.html:
• A data model is the set of tables in your Power BI file and the relationships between them. It is what DAX calculations run against.
  • Most real projects have multiple tables — a Sales table, a Products table, a Customers table, a Date table. The model connects them so you can analyze sales by product, by customer, or by month.
  • You build the model in the Model view (third icon in the left sidebar). Tables appear as boxes; relationships appear as lines connecting them.
  • Simple rule: If all your data is in one table, you have no modeling to do. As soon as you have two tables that share an ID column, you need to define the relationship.

lessons.title: 2. Primary keys and foreign keys
lessons.html:
• Primary key — a column that uniquely identifies each row in a table. No duplicates, no nulls. Example: ProductID in a Products table.
  • Foreign key — a column in another table that references the primary key. Example: ProductID in a Sales table (each sale refers to one product).
  • The relationship connects the primary key table (Products) to the foreign key table (Sales) so Power BI can look up product details for each sale.
  • Trap: If the foreign key column contains values that don't exist in the primary key table, you get a relationship error or missing data in your reports. Always check that IDs match between tables.

lessons.title: 3. Cardinality — one-to-many relationships
lessons.html:
• Cardinality describes how many rows in one table relate to rows in another.
  • One-to-many (1:*): the most common. One product can appear in many sales. The '1' side has unique IDs (Products); the '*' side has repeating IDs (Sales).
    In Model view Power BI shows 1 and * at the ends of the relationship line.
  • Many-to-many (*:*): both tables have repeating values. Requires a bridge table. Avoid in beginner projects.
  • One-to-one (1:1): rare. Each row in table A matches exactly one row in table B.
  • Trap: If you accidentally create a many-to-many relationship where you intended one-to-many, DAX calculations will produce wrong results. Check cardinality in Model view.

lessons.title: 4. Star schema — the standard model structure
lessons.html:
• The star schema is the recommended model structure for Power BI. One central fact table surrounded by dimension tables.
  • Fact table — contains measurements/transactions. Sales amounts, quantities, dates. Many rows, often millions. Example: Sales (OrderID, ProductID, CustomerID, DateID, Amount).
  • Dimension table — describes the entities. Products (ProductID, Name, Category, Price). Customers (CustomerID, Name, City). Dates (DateID, Year, Month, Quarter).
  • Why star schema: DAX calculations are simpler, faster, and more predictable. Filters flow naturally from dimension tables to the fact table.
  • For university TPs: Even with one table you can apply star schema thinking. Split a wide table into a fact table and dimension tables in Power Query.

chapters.title: DAX — measures, calculated columns, and aggregations

lessons.title: 1. What is DAX and when to use it
lessons.html:
• DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is the formula language for calculations in the Power BI data model. You write DAX to create measures and calculated columns.
  • When to use DAX: when you need a calculation that depends on filters, selections, or aggregations across the loaded data. Total sales, % of total, year-over-year growth, running totals.
  • When NOT to use DAX: when you can do it in Power Query instead (cleaning, reshaping, type changes). Power Query runs before loading; DAX runs at query time — DAX on big tables is slower.
  • Rule: If the operation changes the shape or content of a table → Power Query. If it computes a value from existing columns → DAX.

lessons.title: 2. Measures vs calculated columns
lessons.html:
• Measure — a DAX formula that calculates a value dynamically based on whatever filters are active in the report (slicers, page filters, visual filters). It has no fixed value — it recalculates every time the context changes.
  • Example: Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount]) — shows the total for the currently filtered products/dates.
  • Calculated column — a DAX formula that adds a new column to a table. The value is fixed for each row and stored in the model.
  • Example: Profit = Sales[Amount] - Sales[Cost] — adds a Profit column to the Sales table.
  • When to use which: Use measures for aggregations (totals, averages, ratios) that change with filters. Use calculated columns for row-level values that don't depend on filters (category labels, calculated fields per row). Prefer measures — they're more flexible and use less memory.

lessons.title: 3. Basic aggregation functions
lessons.html:
• These are the most-used DAX functions. All work on a column of a table.
  • SUM(Sales[Amount]) — adds all values.
  • AVERAGE(Sales[Amount]) — arithmetic mean.
  • MIN(Sales[Amount]) / MAX(Sales[Amount]) — smallest/largest value.
  • COUNT(Sales[OrderID]) — counts non-blank values in a column.
  • COUNTA(Sales[Product]) — counts non-blank values (works on text too).
  • COUNTROWS(Sales) — counts rows in a table. Use this instead of COUNT on a column when you want row count.
  • DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[ProductID]) — counts unique values.
  • Trap: COUNT ignores blank/null rows. COUNTROWS counts every row including those with blanks. These give different results on tables with nulls.

lessons.title: 4. CALCULATE — the most important DAX function
lessons.html:
• CALCULATE evaluates an expression in a modified filter context. It is the foundation of almost every advanced DAX calculation.
  • Syntax: CALCULATE(expression, filter1, filter2, ...)
  • Example — total sales for Laptops only, regardless of what the slicer shows:
    Laptop Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Product] = "Laptop")
  • Example — sales in January:
    Jan Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Month] = "January")
  • CALCULATE takes the existing filter context and either adds to it, replaces part of it, or removes filters entirely with ALL().
  • Why it matters: Without CALCULATE, every measure is limited to the current filter context. With CALCULATE, you can override filters to compute things like % of total, comparisons, and conditional totals.
  • Trap: CALCULATE with no filter arguments still changes the context — it activates row context transition. This is an advanced concept; for now just use it with explicit filter arguments.

lessons.title: 1. The Report canvas and adding visuals
lessons.html:
• The Report canvas is the blank page where you build your dashboard. It's the default view when you open Power BI Desktop.
  • To add a visual: click a chart type in the Visualizations pane (right side). An empty visual appears on the canvas. Then drag fields from the Fields pane onto the visual's field wells (Axis, Values, Legend, etc.).
  • To resize/move: drag the corners or the title bar of the visual.
  • Pages: add multiple report pages (tabs at the bottom) for different views of the same data.
  • Habit: Don't drag every field onto the canvas and see what happens. Decide first: what question am I answering? Then choose the right visual for that question.

lessons.title: 2. Choosing the right chart type
lessons.html:
• Bar/Column chart — compare values across categories. Bar = horizontal, Column = vertical. Best for most comparisons. Use when you have 2–10 categories.
  • Line chart — show trends over time. Always use for time series (sales over months). Never use for unordered categories.
  • Pie/Donut chart — show parts of a whole. Only useful with 2–4 slices. Avoid with many categories — human eyes can't compare slice sizes accurately. Use a bar chart instead.
  • Card — display a single key number (Total Sales: 142,000). Use for KPIs at the top of a dashboard.
  • Table/Matrix — show detailed data in rows and columns. Matrix supports row/column totals and drill-down like a pivot table.
  • Slicer — an interactive filter the user can click. Add a Month slicer so users can filter all visuals to a specific month.
  • Trap: Pie charts with more than 5 slices are unreadable. Replace with a bar chart sorted descending.

lessons.title: 3. Slicers and filters
lessons.html:
• Slicer — a visual on the canvas that filters other visuals when clicked. Add one by selecting the Slicer visual type, then drag a field (e.g. Month) onto it.
  • Visual-level filter — in the Filters pane, applies only to one specific visual. Useful to show 'Top 5 products' in one chart without affecting others.
  • Page-level filter — applies to all visuals on the current page.
  • Report-level filter — applies to all pages in the report.
  • Cross-filtering: by default, clicking a bar in one chart filters all other visuals on the page. This is automatic — Power BI does it based on the data model relationships.
  • Design rule: Put slicers at the top or left of the page. Users expect filters to be in a consistent location.

lessons.title: 4. Formatting and design principles
lessons.html:
• Format a visual: select it → click the paint roller icon in the Visualizations pane → adjust colors, fonts, labels, borders, background.
  • Data labels: turn them on to show values directly on bars/lines. Turn them off if the chart is too cluttered.
  • Titles: every visual should have a clear, descriptive title that answers the question the visual is addressing. 'Sales' is bad. 'Monthly Sales by Product (2024)' is good.
  • Color: use one consistent color for the same metric across all visuals. Use a highlight color only to draw attention to something important.
  • Less is more: a dashboard with 4 clear visuals is better than one with 12 cluttered ones. Each visual should answer one specific question.
  • Misleading charts: Never start a bar chart Y-axis at anything other than 0 — it exaggerates differences. Never use 3D charts — they distort proportions.

cards.q: What is Power BI Desktop and when do you use it?
cards.out: Power BI Desktop is the Windows application where you build reports — importing data, cleaning it in Power Query, modeling relationships, and creating visuals. You use it to author reports before publishing.
cards.why: Power BI Desktop is the authoring tool. Everything else (Service, Mobile) is for sharing and viewing.

cards.q: Name the 4 stages of a Power BI project in order.
cards.out:
1. Connect — link to data source
2. Transform — clean/reshape in Power Query
3. Model — define table relationships
4. Visualize — build charts and dashboards
cards.why: This order matters. Never skip Transform — dirty data produces wrong visuals.

cards.q: What are the three views in Power BI Desktop's left sidebar?
cards.out:
Report view — build visuals on the canvas
Data view — browse loaded tables
Model view — manage relationships between tables
cards.why: Each view serves a different stage of work. Most time is spent in Report view.

cards.q: What happens if you close the Power Query Editor without clicking 'Close & Apply'?
cards.out: Your changes are discarded — none of the transformations you made are saved to the report.
cards.why: Close & Apply is the commit step. Without it, Power Query changes are temporary.

cards.q:
Complete the M query structure:
___(1)___
    Source = Csv.Document(...),
    Clean = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source)
___(2)___
    Clean
cards.out:
(1) let
(2) in
cards.why: Every M query starts with 'let' (define steps) and ends with 'in StepName' (declare output).

cards.q: When should you use Power Query (M) vs DAX?
cards.out:
Power Query (M): changing the shape or content of data before it loads — cleaning, filtering, pivoting, type changes.
DAX: calculating values from already-loaded data — sums, averages, conditional calculations.
cards.why: Using DAX to do what Power Query should do bloats the model and slows performance.

cards.q: A table has 4 rows and 3 columns. How many cells? What is each row called?
cards.out:
12 cells (4 × 3).
Each row is called a record.
cards.why: Row = record = one complete observation. Column = field = one attribute shared by all records.

cards.q: List 4 Power BI data types and give one example value for each.
cards.out:
Text: 'Laptop'
Whole Number: 42
Decimal Number: 19.99
Date: 2024-01-15
cards.why: Choosing the wrong type blocks calculations. Prices as Text cannot be summed. Dates as Text lose calendar intelligence.

cards.q: What does null mean in Power BI, and how is it different from 0?
cards.out:
null = no value was recorded (absence of data).
0 = a real recorded value of zero.
SUM ignores nulls but includes zeros.
cards.why: Replacing null with 0 is wrong when missing data is not the same as zero sales.

cards.q: Name 3 types of dirty data and how to fix each in Power Query.
cards.out:
1. Inconsistent casing ('laptop' vs 'Laptop') → Transform → Capitalize Each Word
2. Extra spaces (' Laptop') → Transform → Trim
3. Wrong data type (prices as Text) → Change Type → Decimal Number
cards.why: These three issues cause wrong counts, broken relationships, and failed calculations.

cards.q: Your CSV shows all data in one column separated by semicolons. What do you change?
cards.out: Change the delimiter from comma to semicolon in the CSV import dialog (Get Data → Text/CSV → Edit → Delimiter).
cards.why: French/European CSVs use semicolons. Power BI defaults to comma. This is the most common CSV import problem.

cards.q: Which button should you almost always click when importing a file — Load or Transform Data?
cards.out: Transform Data — opens Power Query Editor so you clean and check types before the data loads into the model.
cards.why: Loading without checking often causes type errors and broken calculations that are harder to fix later.

cards.q: What is the difference between Close & Apply and Close in Power Query Editor?
cards.out:
Close & Apply → saves all steps, loads cleaned data into model.
Close → discards all changes since last apply.
cards.why: Closing without Apply is the most common beginner mistake — all cleaning work is lost.

cards.q: Name 3 things you can do with a step in Applied Steps.
cards.out:
1. Click it → preview data at that point
2. Delete it (✕) → remove the transformation
3. Rename it → double-click the name
cards.why: Applied Steps is the undo/debug history of Power Query.

cards.q: What is the difference between Remove Blank Rows and filtering nulls on a specific column?
cards.out:
Remove Blank Rows: removes rows where ALL cells are null.
Filter on column: removes rows where THAT column is null.
Use Filter when a key column has nulls but other columns don't.
cards.why: Remove Blank Rows misses rows with one null in a critical column.

cards.q: What is wide format vs long format? Which does Power BI prefer?
cards.out:
Wide: each category value is a separate column (months as columns).
Long: one column for category name, one for value.
Power BI prefers long — easier to filter, group, and chart.
cards.why: Wide format makes month filtering impossible without unpivoting first.

cards.q: Describe the steps to unpivot the month columns in unpivot.csv.
cards.out:
1. Ctrl+click January, February, March, April
2. Right-click → Unpivot Columns
3. Rename Attribute → Month
4. Rename Value → Sales
Result: 20 rows (5 products × 4 months)
cards.why: Select ONLY month columns — do not include Product or it also becomes rows.

cards.q: Describe the steps to pivot pivot.csv so each month becomes a column.
cards.out:
1. Click the Month column
2. Transform → Pivot Column
3. Values Column = Sales, Aggregate = Sum
Result: 4 rows, one column per month
cards.why: Pivot on Month (the column whose values become headers), not on Sales.

cards.q: After transposing transpose.csv, what two steps are always needed?
cards.out:
1. Home → Use First Row as Headers
2. Rename Column1 to 'Subject'
cards.why: Transpose moves original column headers to row 1. Use First Row as Headers restores them.

cards.q: What are the two keywords that every M query starts and ends with?
cards.out:
let — starts the step definitions block
in StepName — declares which step is the final output
cards.why: Every M query is a let...in expression. 'in' always references the last step you want to load.

cards.q: What does 'each' mean in M, and give one example?
cards.out:
'each' means 'for each row'. It runs the expression once per row.
Example: Table.SelectRows(Source, each [Sales] > 10)
→ keeps only rows where Sales exceeds 10.
cards.why: 'each [Col]' accesses the value of Col in the current row. It's the standard way to write row-level logic in M.

cards.q: What is a star schema? Name its two table types.
cards.out:
Star schema: one central fact table surrounded by dimension tables.
Fact table: measurements/transactions (Sales amounts, quantities).
Dimension table: descriptive attributes (Products, Customers, Dates).
cards.why: Star schema is the standard Power BI model structure. It makes DAX calculations simpler and faster.

cards.q: When should you use a measure vs a calculated column?
cards.out:
Measure: aggregations that change with report filters (Total Sales, % of total).
Calculated column: row-level values fixed per row (Profit = Amount - Cost).
Default choice: measure — more flexible, less memory.
cards.why: Calculated columns are stored in the model and consume memory. Measures are computed on demand.

cards.q: What does CALCULATE do, and give a simple example?
cards.out:
CALCULATE evaluates an expression in a modified filter context.
Example: Laptop Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Product] = "Laptop")
→ Always sums only Laptop sales, overriding any slicer.
cards.why: CALCULATE is the most important DAX function — it lets you control which data the calculation sees.

cards.q:
Match each question to the right chart type:
1. Sales trend over 12 months
2. Sales by product this month
3. Total revenue (one number)
4. Each product's share of total sales
cards.out:
1. Line chart — trends over time
2. Bar/Column chart — compare categories
3. Card — single KPI number
4. Pie chart (only if ≤5 products, else bar chart)
cards.why: Chart type choice depends on what you're communicating: trend, comparison, single value, or proportion.

mcq.q: What are the three products that make up Power BI?
mcq.ok: Power BI Desktop, Power BI Service, Power BI Mobile
bad: Power Query, DAX, Power Pivot
Power BI Desktop, Excel, SQL Server
Power BI Studio, Power BI Online, Power BI App
mcq.why: Power BI Desktop is the Windows authoring tool. Power BI Service is the web publishing platform. Power BI Mobile is the phone viewer.

mcq.q: What are the four stages of a Power BI project in order?
mcq.ok: Connect → Transform → Model → Visualize
bad: Visualize → Model → Transform → Connect
Import → Clean → Report → Publish
Connect → Model → Transform → Visualize
mcq.why: You always connect to data first, then transform/clean it in Power Query, then build the data model, then create visuals. Skipping Transform is the most common beginner mistake.

mcq.q: You receive a CSV from your professor and want to remove blank rows and fix column types before building any chart. Where do you do this?
mcq.ok: Power Query Editor
bad: The Report canvas
The Data view
The Model view
mcq.why: Power Query Editor is the dedicated data-preparation workspace. The Report canvas is for visuals, Data view for browsing loaded data, Model view for relationships.

mcq.q: What is the main advantage of Power BI over Excel for recurring reports?
mcq.ok: Transformations are saved as steps and re-applied automatically when data refreshes
bad: Power BI has more chart types
Power BI formulas are simpler than Excel formulas
Power BI works on Mac and Windows
mcq.why: Power Query records every cleaning step. When new data arrives, all steps replay automatically. In Excel you would re-do the cleaning manually every time.

mcq.q: You click 'Transform Data' in the Home ribbon. What opens?
mcq.ok: The Power Query Editor
bad: The DAX formula editor
The Model view
A new report page
mcq.why: Transform Data is the entry point to Power Query Editor, where data cleaning and reshaping happens.

mcq.q: In Power Query Editor, where do you see every transformation you have applied, in order?
mcq.ok: The Applied Steps pane (Query Settings, right side)
bad: The Formula bar
The Queries pane (left side)
The Data preview (centre)
mcq.why: Applied Steps lists every transformation as a named step. Clicking a step shows the data at that point in the transformation chain.

mcq.q: In M language, what does the 'in' keyword indicate?
mcq.code:
let
    Source = Csv.Document(...),
    Clean = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source)
in
    Clean
mcq.ok: The final step — the output that Power Query returns
bad: The first step — the data source
A loop over each row
An import statement
mcq.why: Every M query ends with 'in StepName'. That step's result is what gets loaded into the model. The 'let' block defines all the intermediate steps.

mcq.q: You need to add up all values in a Sales[Amount] column. Where do you write this and what language do you use?
mcq.ok: In the Data or Report view, using DAX: Total = SUM(Sales[Amount])
bad: In Power Query Editor, using M: Table.Sum(Source, "Amount")
In a cell on the Report canvas, using Excel syntax: =SUM(Amount)
In the Model view, using SQL: SELECT SUM(Amount) FROM Sales
mcq.why: DAX measures are written in the Data or Report view. SUM is a DAX aggregation function. M is for transformations in Power Query, not for calculations in the model.

mcq.q: In a table with 50 rows and 4 columns, how many cells are there?
mcq.why: Cells = rows × columns = 50 × 4 = 200. Each cell holds one value.

mcq.q: Power BI auto-detects a column of product prices as Text instead of Decimal Number. What is the consequence?
mcq.ok: You cannot sum or average the column — calculations will fail or return errors
bad: The column disappears from the Fields pane
Power BI automatically converts it when you use SUM
The column is hidden in the report
mcq.why: Text columns cannot be aggregated mathematically. SUM(Price) on a Text column returns an error. You must change the data type to Decimal Number in Power Query first.

mcq.q: What is the difference between null and 0 in a Sales column?
mcq.ok: null means no data was recorded; 0 means the product sold zero units
bad: They are identical — Power BI treats both as zero
null means the row should be deleted
0 is an error; null is the correct empty value
mcq.why: null = absence of data. 0 = a real recorded value of zero. Treating them the same gives wrong totals and misleading analysis.

mcq.q: Your CSV has 'laptop', 'Laptop', and 'LAPTOP' as values in the Product column. How many distinct products does Power BI see?
mcq.ok: 3 — text comparison is case-sensitive by default
bad: 1 — Power BI normalizes text automatically
2 — it ignores all-caps duplicates
It depends on the data type setting
mcq.why: Power BI treats text as case-sensitive. 'laptop', 'Laptop', and 'LAPTOP' are three different values. Use Transform → Capitalize Each Word or lowercase in Power Query to standardize.

mcq.q: You open a French CSV and all data appears in a single column separated by semicolons. What is the most likely cause?
mcq.ok: The file uses semicolons as delimiters, but Power BI defaulted to comma
bad: The file is corrupted
The encoding is wrong
Power BI cannot read French files
mcq.why: French/European CSV files use semicolons as separators because commas are used as decimal points in French notation. Change the delimiter in the CSV import dialog.

mcq.q: Which of these is an example of structured data?
mcq.ok: A CSV file with columns: OrderID, Product, Amount, Date
bad: A PDF report with paragraphs of text
An email from a client
A folder of product images
mcq.why: Structured data has a defined schema: rows and columns with consistent types. CSVs, Excel tables, and database tables are structured. PDFs, emails, and images are unstructured.

mcq.q: Which data type should you use for a column of dates like '2024-01-15'?
mcq.ok: Date — this enables time-intelligence DAX functions like year-over-year comparison
bad: Text — dates are just strings
Whole Number — dates are stored as numbers internally
Decimal Number — to allow partial days
mcq.why: Power BI's Date type understands calendar hierarchy (year, quarter, month, day) and enables time-intelligence DAX functions. Storing dates as Text loses all of this.

mcq.q: All data from your CSV appears in one column separated by semicolons. What do you change?
mcq.ok: The delimiter in the import dialog — change Comma to Semicolon
bad: The file encoding to UTF-8
Use Transform Data instead of Load
Delete the first row in Power Query
mcq.why: French/European CSVs use semicolons. Power BI defaults to comma. Change the delimiter in the import preview dialog.

mcq.q: What is the difference between Load and Transform Data when importing?
mcq.ok: Load imports immediately with auto-detected types; Transform Data opens Power Query to clean first
bad: They are identical
Load is faster and always correct
Transform Data only works for CSVs
mcq.why: Always use Transform Data so you control types and structure before the data enters the model.

mcq.q: After finishing transformations in Power Query Editor, what do you click?
mcq.ok: Close & Apply (Home tab)
bad: Save (Ctrl+S)
Apply Steps
Close — it auto-saves
mcq.why: Close & Apply commits all steps and loads the cleaned data. Close alone discards your changes.

mcq.q: You click a step in Applied Steps. What happens?
mcq.ok: The data preview updates to show the data at that point in the transformation chain
bad: The step is deleted
The formula bar clears
Power Query reruns from the beginning
mcq.why: Clicking a step is non-destructive. It previews the historical state at that step.

mcq.q: You delete a step that a later step depends on. What happens?
mcq.ok: The later step breaks with a formula error
bad: Power Query auto-updates the later step
The later step is also deleted
Nothing — steps are independent
mcq.why: Each M step references the previous step by name. Deleting a step breaks all steps that reference it.

mcq.q: A Product column has 'laptop', 'Laptop', 'LAPTOP'. What Power Query operation standardizes them?
mcq.ok: Transform → Format → Capitalize Each Word (or Lowercase)
bad: Home → Remove Duplicates
Add Column → Conditional Column
Replace Values three times manually
mcq.why: Format → Capitalize Each Word converts all variants to 'Laptop' in one step.

mcq.q: Remove Blank Rows does not remove a row that has null in Sales but a value in Product. Why?
mcq.ok: Remove Blank Rows only removes rows where ALL columns are null
bad: It doesn't work on numeric columns
The null must be explicitly typed as null first
Power BI treats empty string as not-null
mcq.why: Use Filter Rows on the Sales column specifically to remove rows with null Sales.

mcq.q: unpivot.csv has months as column headers. What operation do you apply?
mcq.code:
Product | January | February | March | April
Laptop  |      10 |       15 |    12 |    18
mcq.ok: Unpivot — select the month columns and unpivot them into rows
bad: Pivot — select Product column and pivot it
Transpose — flip the table
Group By — group by Product
mcq.why: Month names are values, not attributes. Unpivot makes them rows so you can filter by Month in charts.

mcq.q: pivot.csv is in long format (Product, Month, Sales). You want each month as a column. What do you do?
mcq.ok: Select Month column → Transform → Pivot Column → Values Column = Sales
bad: Select Sales column → Unpivot Columns
Transform → Transpose
Add Column → Custom Column with IF
mcq.why: Pivot takes a category column (Month) and spreads its unique values into new columns.

mcq.q: After transposing, the first row contains student names but is treated as data. How do you fix it?
mcq.ok: Home → Use First Row as Headers
bad: Rename each column manually
Home → Remove Top Rows (1)
Add Column → Index Column
mcq.why: Use First Row as Headers promotes the first data row to become column names — always needed after Transpose.

mcq.q: When should you use Transpose instead of Pivot or Unpivot?
mcq.ok: When the entire table is rotated — what should be rows are columns and vice versa
bad: When column headers are category values
When a category column should spread into headers
When you want to aggregate by group
mcq.why: Transpose flips the whole table. Unpivot turns column headers into rows. Pivot turns row values into headers.

mcq.q: In M language, what does 'each [Sales] > 10' mean in this expression?
mcq.ok: For each row, keep it if the Sales column value is greater than 10
bad: Select the column named Sales and filter to values > 10
Sum all Sales values and check if the total exceeds 10
Add a new column with True/False values
mcq.why: 'each' means 'for each row'. [Sales] accesses the Sales column value in that row. The whole expression is a row-level filter condition.

mcq.q: You rename a step from 'Clean' to 'CleanData' in the Advanced Editor. What else must you update?
mcq.ok: Every later step that references 'Clean' by name must be updated to 'CleanData'
bad: Nothing — Power BI auto-updates references
Only the 'in' line at the end
The column names inside the step
mcq.why: M steps reference each other by name. Renaming a step without updating references causes formula errors in all dependent steps.

mcq.q: Which M function adds a new column to a table based on a row-level calculation?
mcq.ok: Table.AddColumn(Source, "NewCol", each [A] * 2)
bad: Table.TransformColumns(Source, {{"A", each _ * 2}})
Table.SelectRows(Source, each [A] * 2)
Table.RenameColumns(Source, {{"A", "NewCol"}})
mcq.why: Table.AddColumn adds a new column. The third argument is a function (using 'each') that runs for every row. TransformColumns modifies an existing column. SelectRows filters rows.

mcq.q: A Products table has ProductID as a unique identifier. A Sales table has ProductID that repeats. What is the relationship type?
mcq.ok: One-to-many: Products (1) → Sales (*)
bad: Many-to-many: both tables have multiple rows
One-to-one: each product has exactly one sale
Many-to-one: Sales (*) → Products (1) is wrong notation
mcq.why: The '1' side has unique IDs (Products). The '*' side has repeating IDs (Sales — one product can have many sales). This is the most common relationship in Power BI models.

mcq.q: In a star schema, what is the fact table?
mcq.ok: The central table containing measurements and transactions (sales amounts, quantities, dates)
bad: The table with the most columns
The dimension table that describes products
The Date table used for time intelligence
mcq.why: Fact tables contain the numbers you measure (sales, costs, counts). Dimension tables describe the entities (products, customers, dates). The fact table is in the centre of the star.

mcq.q: What is the difference between a measure and a calculated column?
mcq.ok: A measure recalculates dynamically based on report filters; a calculated column has a fixed value per row stored in the model
bad: They are identical — both compute values in DAX
A measure is faster; a calculated column is more accurate
Calculated columns work on text; measures only work on numbers
mcq.why: Measures are dynamic — Total Sales changes when you filter by month. Calculated columns are static — Profit = Amount - Cost is computed once per row and stored.

mcq.q: You write SUM(Sales[Amount]). What does this return when a slicer filters to 'January'?
mcq.ok: The sum of Amount for January sales only — the slicer filter is automatically applied
bad: The grand total of all sales regardless of filters
An error — SUM ignores slicers
The count of January rows, not the sum
mcq.why: DAX measures are evaluated in the current filter context. The January slicer adds a filter to the context, so SUM only sums January rows automatically.

mcq.q: What does CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Product] = "Laptop") return?
mcq.ok: The total sales amount for Laptop only, regardless of what other filters are active
bad: The total sales for all products
An error — CALCULATE cannot filter by text
The count of Laptop sales rows
mcq.why: CALCULATE overrides the filter context. Even if a slicer shows all products, this measure always filters to Laptop before summing.

mcq.q: You want to show sales trends over 12 months. Which chart type is most appropriate?
mcq.ok: Line chart — designed for showing trends over time
bad: Pie chart — shows the proportion each month contributes
Bar chart — good for comparing categories but not ideal for time trends
Card — shows a single number, not a trend
mcq.why: Line charts are designed for time series. The continuous line makes trends and patterns visible. Bar charts work for category comparisons but don't show continuity over time.

mcq.q: A slicer on your report page shows months. A user clicks 'March'. What happens to the other visuals?
mcq.ok: All visuals on the page update to show only March data
bad: Only the slicer itself updates — other visuals are unaffected
Only visuals that have a Date field update
The page reloads from the data source
mcq.why: Slicers apply a page-level filter context. All visuals on the page that use data from the same model tables will respond to the filter automatically.

mcq.q: Your bar chart Y-axis starts at 950 instead of 0. What is the problem?
mcq.ok: It visually exaggerates the differences between bars — small differences look huge
bad: It is more accurate because it shows the relevant range
It is a Power BI default that cannot be changed
It only matters for pie charts, not bar charts
mcq.why: Bar chart length is the visual encoding of the value. If the axis doesn't start at 0, a bar that's 5% taller than another looks 10x taller. Always start bar/column chart axes at 0.

boards.title: Power BI in 4 steps — the full workflow

steps.say: Before touching any button in Power BI, you need to understand the four stages every project goes through. This is the map — learn it and you'll never be lost.
add: {b:Stage 1 — Connect} Link Power BI to your data: a CSV file, an Excel file, a website, a database.
{b:Stage 2 — Transform} Open Power Query Editor. Clean the data: fix types, remove blanks, rename columns, reshape.
{b:Stage 3 — Model} Define how tables relate to each other (like a sales table linked to a products table by Product ID).
{b:Stage 4 — Visualize} Drag fields onto the canvas. Choose chart types. Add slicers. Build the dashboard.

The most skipped stage:
Stage 2 — Transform.
Dirty data = wrong visuals.
Always clean before you build.

steps.say: Here's how to open each stage in the real software. Memorize where each tool lives.
add: Where to find each stage in Power BI Desktop
{b:Connect} → Home ribbon → Get Data → choose your file type
{b:Transform} → Home ribbon → Transform Data → opens Power Query Editor
{b:Model} → Left sidebar → Model view icon (third icon)
{b:Visualize} → Left sidebar → Report view icon (first icon, default)

Transform Data button
is in the Home ribbon.
This opens Power Query Editor.
Remember this — it's where
all cleaning happens.

add.q: Your professor gave you a CSV with messy column names and wrong data types. Which stage do you work in first?
add.ok: Stage 2 — Transform, in Power Query Editor
bad: Stage 4 — Visualize, fix it in the chart settings
Stage 3 — Model, change types in the relationship view
Stage 1 — Connect, re-import with different settings
add.why: Data type errors and column names are cleaned in Power Query (Stage 2). You must fix them before the data loads into the model.

steps.say: Now let's lock in the difference between M and DAX — two languages, two totally different jobs.
add: M vs DAX — two languages, different jobs
{b:M (Power Query)} runs BEFORE data loads. Changes the shape and content of tables.
{b:DAX} runs AFTER data loads. Calculates values from existing columns.

-- M example (Power Query, reshaping):
Table.RemoveColumns(Source, {"Junk"})

-- DAX example (measure, calculation):
Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])

If the question is
'what does the table look like?'
→ Power Query (M).
If the question is
'what does this number equal?'
→ DAX.

add.q: You want to calculate the average sale amount per product. Which language do you use?
add.ok: DAX — write a measure: Avg Sale = AVERAGE(Sales[Amount])
bad: M — add a custom column in Power Query with the average
SQL — query the table directly
Neither — use a chart aggregation setting instead
add.why: DAX measures calculate values from loaded data. AVERAGE is a DAX function. Power Query M is for transforming the table structure, not for business calculations.

boards.title: Data types and dirty data — the hidden cause of wrong answers

steps.say: Most Power BI errors aren't about formulas — they're about data types. A price column stored as Text is the most common cause of broken calculations in university TPs.
add: {b:Text} → words, names, codes. 'Laptop', 'Ahmed'. Cannot do math.

Power BI auto-detects types
on import and often gets
prices wrong (Text instead
of Decimal). Always check
the type icon on each column.

steps.say: Now the three dirty-data problems that appear in almost every TP. Recognize them and fix them in Power Query.
add: {b:Fix:} Transform tab → Format → Capitalize Each Word (or Lowercase).
{b:Problem 3 — Wrong data type:} Sales amounts stored as Text.
{b:Fix:} Click the column header type icon → change to Decimal Number.

null ≠ 0.
null = no data recorded.
0 = sold zero units.
Never replace null
with 0 without checking.

add.q: Your SUM(Sales[Amount]) measure returns an error. The most likely cause is?
add.ok: The Amount column has data type Text instead of Decimal Number
bad: The measure formula is wrong — SUM needs two arguments
The Sales table is not in the model
The column name has a space in it
add.why: SUM only works on numeric columns. If Amount is Text, DAX cannot aggregate it. Fix the type in Power Query Editor before closing and applying.

boards.title: Pivot, Unpivot, Transpose — with your professor's actual CSV data

steps.say: Your professor gave you three CSV files, each designed for one specific transformation. Let's work through each one — not just the how, but the why.
add: {b:unpivot.csv} → needs Unpivot (wide→long). Months are column headers — they're values.
{b:pivot.csv} → needs Pivot (long→wide). Months are row values — spread them into columns.
{b:transpose.csv} → needs Transpose. The whole table is oriented the wrong way.

The filenames tell you the
operation. In real TPs
you'll need to judge yourself
from the data shape.

steps.say: Start with unpivot.csv. Months are column headers — but months are values, not attributes. Here's the problem and the fix.
add:
BEFORE (wide — 5 rows):
Product  | January | February | March | April
Laptop   |      10 |       15 |    12 |    18
Mouse    |      30 |       25 |    40 |    35

AFTER (long — 20 rows):
Product  | Month    | Sales
Laptop   | January  |    10
Laptop   | February |    15
Mouse    | January  |    30
{b:Steps:} Ctrl+click January, February, March, April → right-click → Unpivot Columns → rename Attribute→Month, Value→Sales.

Select ONLY the month columns.
If you include Product,
it also becomes rows — wrong.

add.q: After unpivoting (5 products × 4 months), how many rows does the result have?
bad: 5 rows — one per product
4 rows — one per month
9 rows — 5 + 4
add.why: Unpivot creates one row per combination. 5 products × 4 months = 20 rows.

steps.say: Now pivot.csv — already long format, but you need months as columns for a comparison table.
add:
BEFORE (long — 12 rows):
Product  | Month    | Sales
Laptop   | January  |    10
Laptop   | February |    15
Mouse    | January  |    30

AFTER (wide — 4 rows):
Product  | January | February | March
Laptop   |      10 |       15 |    12
Mouse    |      30 |       25 |    40
{b:Steps:} Click Month column → Transform → Pivot Column → Values Column: Sales → OK.

Pivot on the column whose
values become headers (Month).
Not on the values column (Sales).

add.q: When would you choose 'Don't Aggregate' in the Pivot dialog?
add.ok: When each product-month combination appears exactly once — no duplicates
bad: Always — aggregation is optional
When the values column contains text
When you want to sum all values
add.why: Don't Aggregate fails if any combination appears more than once. Use Sum when duplicates exist.

steps.say: Finally transpose.csv — subjects should be rows but they're currently columns. Transpose flips the whole table.
add:
BEFORE:
Student | Math | Physics | Computer Science
Ahmed   |   15 |      14 |               18
Sara    |   17 |      16 |               19

AFTER (then promote headers):
Subject          | Ahmed | Sara | Youssef | Mariam
Math             |    15 |   17 |      12 |     18
Physics          |    14 |   16 |      13 |     17
Computer Science |    18 |   19 |      15 |     20
{b:Steps:} Transform → Transpose → Home → Use First Row as Headers → rename Column1 to Subject.

After every Transpose:
Use First Row as Headers.
The original column names
move to row 1 during transpose.

add.q: After transposing, the first column is named 'Column1' and contains subject names. What two steps fix this?
add.ok: Use First Row as Headers (promotes row 1), then rename Column1 to 'Subject'
bad: Delete Column1, then add a new column
Transpose again to undo
Replace Values: Column1 → Subject
add.why: Transpose moves original headers to row 1. Use First Row as Headers promotes them back. Then rename the leftmost column.

boards.title: DAX from zero — measures, SUM, and CALCULATE

steps.say: DAX is what makes Power BI smart. Without it your report shows raw data. With it you can answer questions like 'what percentage of total sales does each product represent?' Let's build from zero.
add:
-- Click on the Sales table in the Fields pane
-- Home ribbon → New Measure
-- Type this formula:

Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])

-- Press Enter. The measure appears in the Sales table with a calculator icon.
{b:SUM(Sales[Amount])} — adds every value in the Amount column of the Sales table.
Drag Total Sales onto the canvas → it shows the grand total. Add a Product slicer → it automatically filters to the selected product.

Measures live in a table
but have no rows.
They recalculate every time
the filter context changes.

steps.say: Now the most important DAX function — CALCULATE. It lets you override what the slicer shows and compute values for a specific subset of data.
add:
-- Sales for Laptops only (ignores slicers):
Laptop Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Product] = "Laptop")

-- % of total:
% of Total = DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALL(Sales)))
{b:ALL(Sales)} removes all filters from the Sales table — so the denominator is always the grand total.
{b:DIVIDE(a, b)} is safer than a/b — it returns 0 instead of an error when b is 0.

CALCULATE = 'compute this
expression, but with
these filters instead.'

add.q: A slicer filters to March. What does CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALL(Sales)) return?
add.ok: The grand total of ALL sales — CALCULATE with ALL() removes the March filter
bad: Only March sales — the slicer still applies
An error — ALL() cannot be used inside CALCULATE
Zero — ALL() clears the data
add.why: ALL() removes all filters from the specified table. CALCULATE then evaluates SUM in that context — which is the full dataset, ignoring the slicer.
